title: Top incidents analysis (last 2 quarters) — clustering + candidate taxonomy (working)
content:
Working doc for Incident taxonomy + ownership mapping (Reliability Program).

Scope
- Time window: last 2 quarters (approx 2025-07-01 through 2025-10-31). Data pulled 2025-11-18.
- Sources included:
  - incident-bot incidents (Sev0–Sev3) from #incidents
  - postmortems and “mini-RCA” docs when available
  - support escalations tagged “incident” (Jira SUP) and CS escalation summaries
  - a small set of internal high-severity near-misses (where we had to page / roll back)
- Sources excluded (for now): pure security incidents (handled separately), planned maintenance, load tests/synthetic alerts with no user impact.

What this is for
- Identify the highest-volume / highest-impact symptom clusters.
- Propose a bounded v1 taxonomy (10–15 top-level categories, low-cardinality subtypes).
- Call out data-quality gaps that will block accurate reporting unless fixed (naming, severity, tier attribution, duplicate incident records).

Quick headline takeaways (directional)
1) Overload/5xx + capacity constraints are still the dominant *customer-visible* incident pattern, especially during regional pressure events.
2) Latency regressions are the most common “slow burn” incident class and are under-tracked because they often start as alerts and only become incidents after CS escalation.
3) Streaming disconnects are a distinct class with mixed ownership (gateway/network vs client behavior). We need crisp boundaries for taxonomy.
4) Routing/fallback issues are overrepresented in “multi-cause” incidents (capacity + routing policy + health signals). v1 must define the “primary incident type” rule.
5) Control plane outages are fewer in count but high in severity for Dedicated/Private because they block config changes and recovery actions.

Methodology notes
- I started from incident-bot export: incident title, timestamps, severity, tier, impacted regions, and freeform summary.
- I normalized symptoms into a “symptom label” for clustering (manual + light heuristics): 5xx spike, p95 latency, streaming resets, 429/throttling, auth failures, control plane write errors, routing/fallback anomalies, capacity alarms, telemetry gaps, private connectivity.
- Clustering is rough and based on symptom + immediate mitigation playbook used (e.g., “failover”, “scale fleet”, “rollback model”, “disable canary policy”).
- The counts below are *incidents*, not alerts. Some incidents have multiple symptoms; I recorded a “primary symptom” and listed secondaries in notes.

Data quality flags (high confidence issues)
- Duplicate incidents: ~6–10% likely duplicates due to incident re-open / re-page / multiple channels created for same event.
- Tier attribution missing or inconsistent: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private not consistently recorded; Dedicated incidents sometimes filed as Hosted when only the shared gateway was impacted.
- Severity drift: Sev1 vs Sev2 varies by IC and by time of day; some “Sev2 but 2+ hours of partial outage” cases.
- Incident title / freeform text quality: too many incident titles like “API errors” or “latency” with no model/region/service clue.
- Missing mitigation timestamps: start/mitigated/resolved not always captured → MTTR analysis is noisy.
- Support escalations not linked: SUP tickets often reference “ongoing incident” but do not include incident ID; back-linking required for accurate total impact.

Dataset summary (after light dedupe)
- Total incidents in window (Sev0–Sev3): 128
  - Sev0: 6
  - Sev1: 22
  - Sev2: 51
  - Sev3: 49
- Tier attribution (best-effort):
  - Hosted: 79
  - Dedicated: 33
  - Private: 16
- Regions most frequently referenced (not exhaustive): us-east, us-west, eu-central. (APAC data incomplete due to different on-call notes in some cases.)

Top symptom clusters (incidents; primary symptom)
NOTE: Primary symptom is “what the customer saw / what paged first”, not necessarily root cause.

| Rank | Symptom cluster (primary)                         | Count | Typical secondary symptom(s)                         | Notes |
|------|---------------------------------------------------|-------|------------------------------------------------------|------|
| 1    | 5xx / request failures / overload                 | 31    | 429s, elevated queue depth, fallback activation       | Mix of true overload, regional failover, bad routing health |
| 2    | Latency regression (p95/p99)                      | 24    | timeouts, partial 5xx, client retries                | Often tied to rollout, runtime regressions, or noisy neighbor |
| 3    | Capacity / fleet shortages                        | 18    | increased fallbacks, elevated latency, 429 throttling | GPU provisioning lag, regional saturation, quota vs capacity confusion |
| 4    | Streaming disconnects / resets                    | 14    | latency spikes, gateway errors                        | Boundary unclear: client SDK behavior vs gateway vs network |
| 5    | Routing / fallback misbehavior                    | 12    | 5xx spikes, wrong model/region selection              | Includes policy misconfig + health signal bugs |
| 6    | Control plane outage / config write failures       | 9     | delayed mitigation, inability to flip routing         | High impact in Dedicated/Private recovery workflows |
| 7    | Auth/RBAC failures (tokens, perms, key rotation)   | 7     | 401/403 spikes, login issues                          | Some overlap with Security Ops triggers |
| 8    | Telemetry blind spot (metrics/logs/tracing broken) | 6     | delayed detection, paging gaps                         | Not always customer-impacting but increases MTTR |
| 9    | Private connectivity/config issues (DNS/TLS/VPC)   | 5     | intermittent timeouts, handshake errors               | Often upgrade-related; high support involvement |
| 10   | Dependency/provider event (cloud region/network)   | 2     | multi-region failover, packet loss                     | Low count but high confusion during classification |

Support escalations (Jira SUP) that map strongly to clusters
- SUP-18421 intermittent 500s during region failover → 5xx/overload + routing/failover interplay.
- SUP-18703 streaming disconnects after SDK upgrade → streaming disconnects; also suggests need for client-vs-platform boundary.
- SUP-19112 429s and throttling on Dedicated burst → quota enforcement vs capacity saturation; likely capacity/fleet subtype + rate limiting policy.
- SUP-19388 latency regression on model version rollout → latency regression + rollout regression subtype.
- SUP-19745 private DNS/TLS errors after upgrade → private connectivity/config class.
- SUP-20106 control plane config write failures → control plane outage class.

Candidate taxonomy categories (v1 proposal inputs)
Goal: low-cardinality, “usable during incident”, maps to owner boundaries, supports reporting.

Proposed top-level categories (10–12)
1) Availability: 5xx / request failures
2) Latency degradation (p95/p99 regression)
3) Streaming/session instability (disconnects, resets)
4) Routing & fallback behavior (wrong target, fallback loops, policy mismatch)
5) Capacity & fleet health (GPU shortages, provisioning lag, saturation)
6) Control plane reliability (config read/write failures, policy propagation)
7) Auth & access control (API keys, tokens, RBAC, org/project perms)
8) Observability & telemetry gaps (metrics/logs/tracing missing or wrong)
9) Private deployment connectivity & config (DNS/TLS/VPC routing, on-prem edge)
10) Rollout regression (model/runtime/config rollout causing degradation)
11) External dependency event (cloud provider / upstream outage)
12) Tooling/process incident (incident-bot/paging misroutes blocking response) — optional; may keep as “contributing factor” rather than primary

Candidate subtypes (example list; not final)
- Availability:
  - Overload/queue saturation
  - Gateway 5xx
  - Runtime crash/OOM
  - Rate limiting/throttle misconfiguration (if user-visible failures)
- Latency:
  - Runtime regression (scheduler stalls, KV cache thrash)
  - Capacity pressure (queueing)
  - Model-specific perf regression
  - Dependency latency (storage/control plane)
- Streaming:
  - Gateway streaming resets
  - Network instability (suspected)
  - Client incompatibility (if confirmed; else “unknown”)
- Routing/fallback:
  - Health signal bug
  - Policy misconfig
  - Fallback loop / excessive fallback
  - Incorrect region selection
- Capacity/fleet:
  - Provisioning lag
  - Regional saturation
  - Autoscaling failure
  - GPU node health/failure domain
- Control plane:
  - Policy propagation delay
  - Config write/read outage
  - Control plane DB/queue backlog
- Auth:
  - Token issuance/validation
  - RBAC/permission regression
  - Key rotation/expiry
- Observability:
  - Metrics pipeline outage
  - Log ingestion gaps
  - Alert misfire/noise (if it materially impacted response)
- Private:
  - DNS resolution
  - TLS/cert/handshake
  - VPC routing / firewall
  - Upgrade/config drift
- Rollout regression:
  - Model version rollout
  - Runtime release
  - Routing config rollout
- External dependency:
  - Cloud provider region outage
  - Network provider event

Notes on multi-cause incidents (important for classification policy)
- Roughly 30–40% of Sev0/Sev1 incidents in this window have multiple plausible “types” (capacity + routing + failover is the common trio).
- Recommendation for v1 classification rule:
  - Choose primary incident type based on “what lever was most responsible for mitigation” OR “what system we control that failed first”, then list 1–3 contributing systems/types.
  - Example: regional saturation triggers fallback; fallback misbehaves and amplifies → primary could be Routing/fallback (if bug), contributing Capacity.

Where the data doesn’t support fine-grained taxonomy (yet)
- Streaming disconnect root cause attribution is weak; most incidents ended with “likely client retries” or “suspect network” without confirming evidence.
- Capacity events often lack a consistent definition between “quota enforcement” vs “true fleet exhaustion”. We need a clear signal-based boundary.
- Latency incidents rarely specify: “inference runtime vs gateway vs dependency”; we need better per-hop latency breakdown and consistent incident templates.

Suggested metrics/labels to enable taxonomy (instrumentation asks)
- Add structured fallback_reason enums (capacity/health/policy/timeout) to routing metrics/logs.
- Add request_error class (“gateway_5xx”, “runtime_oom”, “timeout”, “auth_denied”) with allowlisted values.
- Require incident-bot fields: tier, region(s), affected surface (chat/embeddings/streaming), incident_type/subtype.
- Cardinality guardrail: keep incident_type to an allowlist; do NOT auto-emit raw strings into metrics labels.

Open questions / follow-ups for taxonomy workshop
1) Should “Rollout regression” be primary type or always a subtype under Availability/Latency/etc?
2) Where do we put “429s” when customer sees throttling: Auth/Rate limiting vs Capacity? (I suggest: primary = Capacity if fleet constrained; primary = Auth/Rate limiting if policy misconfig.)
3) How to handle “external dependency” events: do we want a top-level type, or tag as contributing factor only?
4) Private: do we want separate types for “Private control plane” vs “Private networking” or keep as one with subtypes?

Next actions (for Reliability Program)
- [Mei] Provide raw incident list w/ proposed cluster labels + confidence score (for backfill; separate doc/sheet).
- [Rafael] Align proposed top-level categories with owner boundaries (Routing vs Fleet vs Control Plane vs Runtime).
- [Allison] Review metric labeling proposal for cardinality risk; propose allowlist schema.
- [Dev] Validate the top 10 clusters against Support escalations (are we missing recurring pain?)

Appendix: example mapping from symptom → candidate taxonomy
- 5xx spike + GPU saturation alerts + mitigation = add capacity → Capacity & fleet health (primary), Availability (secondary)
- p95 latency up after model rollout + rollback fixes → Rollout regression (primary) OR Latency degradation w/ subtype “model rollout” (decision pending)
- streaming disconnects after SDK upgrade + no server-side errors → Streaming instability (primary), contributing factor “client incompatibility”
- customer cannot update routing policies + control plane 5xx → Control plane reliability (primary)

Changelog
- 2025-11-18: initial export + first-pass clustering.
- 2025-11-25: added tier split + support ticket cross-reference; adjusted symptom definitions.
- 2025-12-02: added candidate taxonomy section + open questions for workshop.
